options: The support force a surface pushes back with, perpendicular to itself
The pull of gravity toward the center
The friction that stops motion
The bounce in a ball
questions.explanation: The normal force is the upturned support a surface provides — perpendicular (at 90°) to the surface.
questions.misconception: It commonly gets reduced to 'the weight' or to friction; it's the perpendicular push from the surface itself.

questions.prompt: A book sits flat on a table. Which direction does the table's normal force point?
options: Straight up, perpendicular to the tabletop
Straight down
Along the table to the left
Anywhere it chooses
questions.explanation: Normal means perpendicular — the push comes straight out of the tabletop, i.e. upward in this flat case.
questions.misconception: Some think the surface pushes along itself or downward; the defining quirk is the 90° angle, never along the surface.

questions.prompt: On flat ground, why doesn't a resting book fall through the table?
options: The normal force pushes up with a force equal to the book's weight
The table secretly glues it in place
Air keeps the book suspended
The book is too wide to fall
questions.explanation: The surface pushes upward with a normal force matching the downward weight — the two cancel, so the book stays put.
questions.misconception: It's easy to read the table as just 'solid stuff'; the physics is the perpendicular support force exactly matching the weight.

questions.prompt: A ball rests on a ramp tilted 30°. Compared with flat ground, the normal force is...
options: Smaller, because only part of the weight presses into the slope
Bigger, because ramps push harder
Exactly the same as on flat
Zero, ramps have no normal force
questions.explanation: On a tilted surface, part of the weight acts along the slope, so the perpendicular support needed (and given) is smaller.
questions.misconception: A fixed 'equals weight always' rule gets broken by the ramp — the equal value happens only on flat ground.

questions.prompt: An elevator starts accelerating upward. The floor's normal force on you becomes...
options: Stronger — it must accelerate you upward too
Weaker — you feel lighter
Zero the whole time
Exactly equal forever
questions.explanation: To accelerate you upward, the floor must supply an extra upward push via the normal force — that extra push is what you feel pressing against your feet.
questions.misconception: The classic feeling is 'heavier' — but the mass doesn't change; it's the normal force spiking upward to accelerate you.
